claims.text: Premelting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by nanoscale chemical segregation.
Clustering or local enrichment of Cu is the segregation feature chiefly responsible for premelting.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other constituents of the stated alloy.
Cu-enriched regions have reduced local melting temperatures.
Low-melting Cu-enriched regions initiate premelting before the bulk solid solution melts.
Rapid solidification produces Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles with a near-uniform elemental distribution.
Cooling rate can alter the phase or structural state of a high-entropy alloy.
Varying cooling rate controls the extent of nanoscale chemical segregation in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Slower cooling promotes Cu segregation in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
The resulting Cu-rich inhomogeneities lower the local effective melting temperature.
Slower-cooled, more Cu-segregated nanoparticles will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than rapidly cooled homogeneous nanoparticles.
Rapidly cooled homogeneous baseline nanoparticles exhibit a higher and more uniform premelting-onset temperature.
A controlled atmosphere and gradual heating ramp ensure that observed transitions are solely due to intrinsic thermal behavior.
The proposed mechanism may cease to govern when amorphization or particle-size-related effects dominate.
Interactions among the other elements or nanoparticle size-dependent stresses may also contribute to premelting.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field characterizes the nanoparticles generally as homogeneous and produced by rapid solidification, whereas the controlled comparison requires a second, slower-cooled population that is intentionally segregated. The initial-state description therefore does not consistently cover both experimental groups.
